Who’s ready for coaching? 7 GLP-1 clients, from “not yet” to “let’s go!”

📅 11 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 22 min read (4471 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Precisionnutrition

⏱️ ~22 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • That’s the thought many health and fitness coaches had when GLP-1 medications first hit the mass market.
  • Though semaglutide (Ozempic) became available in 2017, it initially felt like a theoretical threat.
  • Now, in 2026, over 1 in 10 US adults are taking a GLP-1 medication.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Reviewed by Brian St. Pierre, MS, RD.

That’s the thought many health and fitness coaches had when GLP-1 medications first hit the mass market.

Though semaglutide (Ozempic) became available in 2017, it initially felt like a theoretical threat. Prescription rates were still very low, and it seemed like no one actually knew anyone who was taking it.

Now, in 2026, over 1 in 10 US adults are taking a GLP-1 medication. Most of us know someone on it (or we’re on it ourselves).

With wider use, opinions towards the medication have softened too. Most coaches no longer see it as a threat, and instead appreciate it as a valuable tool for certain clients, with coaching as an additive complement.

Many coaches still have concerns though, primarily about their clients’ long term health on the medication. (Among the worries: Loss of muscle mass! Using a “band-aid” solution! Bypassing foundational health habits! And more!).

However, whether you count yourself as a GLP-1 supporter or a GLP-1 skeptic, there’s a framing that might change the way you think about your work in this field:.

As Kate Solovieva, Super Coach and PN’s Director of Community, says: “As a coach, you’re not in the GLP-1 world; you’re in the GLP-1 support world.”.

In a recent development, that’s actually good news. Because trying to coach everyone taking a GLP-1 just isn’t possible. And spending time thinking about all the people using GLP-1s “the wrong way” is, bluntly, wasted energy. Some of those people just don’t want, need, or aren’t ready for your help.

Meanwhile, there is a subgroup of people on GLP-1s who are ready, willing, and able to receive your support. Honing in on this group is where you can actually make a difference (and where your business can thrive).

Sources indicate that in the following article, we’ll cover seven GLP-1 clients you’re likely to meet. Each reflects a different point in the GLP-1 medication journey, and a different level of readiness for coaching. Based on our experience coaching over 175,000 clients (of which an increasing number are on GLP-1s), we’ll offer strategies to work with each.

Before we begin, a reminder: People change, and readiness isn’t fixed.

A person who starts off saying “I’m doing fine on my own” may eventually morph into “I’m flailing and really need someone else in my corner”—and vice versa.

If the person in front of you sounds like one of these clients, that’s where they are right now. So listen carefully to how your client speaks at every session, and respond dynamically.

In general, Coach Kate says someone is usually ready for coaching when they demonstrate two things:.

Keep that in the back of your mind as you interact with client prospects, and as you read about each client, summarized in the table below.

Now, on to the different GLP-1 clients.

This is the person who’s started a GLP-1 medication—and they love it.

They’ve experienced minimal side effects, and have gotten great results on a relatively low dose.

They haven’t changed much about their exercise habits or their diet (except the eating less part, which the medication has taken care of), but they’re seeing what they want to see on the scale, so they don’t feel motivated to change anything.

It might be tempting to “lure” this kind of client in by warning them of the dangers of using a GLP-1 medication without adding in long-term health behaviors (like resistance training and strategic nutrition), but this type of approach can backfire.

At best, you may sound like a downer. At worst, you may sound like an active antagonist.

According to recent reports, in Motivational Interviewing, a communication approach commonly used in coaching, this is called the “righting reflex.” It’s the urge that coaches, counselors, and therapists often have to help or “correct course” for their client. You see them doing something “wrong,” and you want to help them “fix” it.

However, following this instinct may actually strengthen a client’s defenses, and prevent change.

If a person is flying high on their current approach, their readiness for coaching is extremely low.

As Coach Kate indicates, “they’re just not my person yet.”.

Your best move with this client is to genuinely celebrate their current results, then plant the seed for support should they need it in the future.

According to recent reports, for example, you could say: “It must feel so good to see all these positive results! If you ever feel like you want to work on another layer, like resistance training or optimizing your nutrition, I’d love to work together.”.

Sources indicate that then, just stay available. (“My door is always open!”).

This is the person who hasn’t started a GLP-1 medication—and might never, despite being a great candidate for one.

Maybe their doctor has already suggested the medication to them and they’ve read everything they can on the topic.

And yet, they’re frozen with fear at the starting line. They’re afraid of side effects, of being on medication for life, of not holding up their end of the bargain. (“I’ve been trying to start strength training for years. If I take this medication it matters even more… What if I still can’t do it?”).

Toni Bauer, Super Coach and PN’s Director of Coaching and Education Operations also says that, in some cases, a client’s hesitation isn’t about side effects. “Some of our clients wonder, ‘Am I a good person or a bad person if I start taking a GLP-1 medication? Am I weak? Am I giving up?’” Coach Toni says these concerns aren’t unique to GLP-1 medications, but they seem to be especially common.

According to recent reports, she reasons, “If you have high cholesterol, are you weak for taking cholesterol medication? No. But often people don’t view obesity as a disease at a societal level, so the conversation is different here.”.

Regardless of the root cause of this person’s hesitation, the advice below can help them find clarity.

First, let’s be clear: Deciding whether or not to take a medication isn’t a coaching decision, and falls out of your scope of practice. That choice is ultimately up to your client and a medical provider who can assess whether a GLP-1 is appropriate given their medical history.

That remarked, clients may still come to you wanting to discuss their options.

So the question becomes: How do you support someone through a decision you can’t make for them?

Recent findings suggest that coach Toni advises: “You can share facts and data. For example, study results and what you’ve seen with other clients. But you can’t say, ‘For you, this is the right choice.’”.

Instead, the biggest coaching opportunity here is to help clients articulate what’s actually driving their hesitation.

This hesitation about whether to do something different or stay the same is called ambivalence, and it’s a normal (albeit uncomfortable) stage of change.

Problem is, without the right tools, a person can stay stuck in ambivalence for months or even years. And, much like being stuck at an airport in between two destinations, it sucks.

But at PN, we have a cool exercise to deal with client ambivalence. It’s called the 4 Crazy Questions. Essentially, you explore:.

In this context, the questions can help a client explore the risk of starting a GLP-1 (which they’ve probably already voiced), but also the risk of not starting, which they may not have considered yet.

Our 4 Crazy Questions worksheet can encourage clients to explore the pros and cons of both choices. With these considerations laid out explicitly, most people feel a lot more clear about their next steps—or at least what questions they need to ask their medical provider before they can move forward.

According to recent reports, importantly, this exercise doesn’t have a “right” outcome. Some people work through it and fill the prescription. Others decide the medication isn’t for them, and that’s fine. (It’s also worth reminding clients that starting isn’t necessarily permanent: With their provider’s input, a trial run on the medication is a perfectly valid way in.).

According to recent reports, either way, there are opportunities to support your client. As Coach Toni puts it: “Whether you go ‘natural’ or whether you go GLP-1, the foundational habits are essentially the same.”.

This is the person who started a GLP-1 with lots of optimism—and now feels like they have a plague that won’t end.

In a cruel twist, this person might actually be seeing great fat loss results. And yet, they’re nauseated, exhausted, dreading their next dose, and wondering whether it’s worth continuing this medication.

Adding to their sense of defeat, they may also be comparing themselves to a “Honeymooner” in their life, so they might also be wondering if there’s something wrong with them. (“It worked so well for my friend! I must be broken in some way.”).

First, offer some neutral education to depersonalize their experience.

Recent findings suggest that namely, they should know that side effects are extremely common: About half of users report nausea, a third report diarrhea, and a fifth report vomiting.1 So, what this person thinks is exceptional might actually just be a normal adjustment. (This doesn’t make the experience suck less, but it can give them some hope.).

Also, getting GLP-1s right is a process of trial and error: the right medication, the right dose, and the right nutritional strategies to reduce symptoms.

Industry observers note that if their symptoms are severe, get them to loop in their doctor. Medication type and dosing is under the purview of a medical professional, so involving them is essential.

After that, your best coaching move is to suggest an experiment.

Recent findings suggest that ▶ Ask about dose. To be clear, you’re asking about it, not adjusting it. Says Coach Toni: “Often, when people are experiencing extreme side effects, they’ve ratcheted up their dose too quickly. Sometimes the easiest way to keep somebody on a GLP-1 who’s experiencing high side effects is to lower their dosage.” Coach Toni makes clear that while dosage isn’t a coach’s domain, you can help draw a client’s attention to it.

▶ Start a food journal. It doesn’t need to be every day—just around the meals that precede the worst symptoms. You’re looking for three things:.

In a recent development, ▶ Try smaller portions, eaten more often. Coach Toni says if you only try one thing, this one is the most reliable strategy. GLP-1 clients may be tempted to cut meals when symptoms are high, but this increases the likelihood of undereating and nutrient deficiencies. The goal, in her words: “Can we get small enough, frequent enough meals that we get nutrients in, but they never feel overwhelmed or super full?”.

To stay within your scope of practice, language matters.

Don’t say: “You’re nauseous, so you should eat smaller meals.”.

Instead, say: “Folks who are nauseous sometimes do better with smaller, more frequent meals. Want to try it this week and see what you notice?”.

In the first example, you’ve offered a “prescription” (which coaches can’t legally do). In the second example, you’ve offered an experiment to consider.

According to recent reports, side effects (such as nausea, vomiting, constipation, and/or diarrhea) are extremely common among GLP-1 owners, and typically last one to two weeks after initiating the medication. Some symptoms can last longer (particularly constipation), but most are mild to moderate, and usually improve within a few weeks.

Symptoms can also return each time a dosage is increased, though they’re usually milder and more short-lived. These too tend to improve after the first week or so.

However, you should strongly encourage a client to reach out promptly to their medical provider if they notice:.

Reassure your client they’re not being dramatic by reporting these symptoms. Their medical team needs to hear this kind of information to help them get the best results, while preserving overall health.

Also: Your client will get better care if they show up prepared. So, get them to jot down and bring:.

This is the person whose results look great, but less visible changes are creating longer term risks.

This person is likely to be quite sedentary, and when you ask what they do for exercise, they might tell you “I walk.” But they’re not the outlier kind of walker who consistently gets 20,000 steps a day. They just… walk a little.

Women are more likely to fall into this category, especially if they come from a generation or culture where strength training simply wasn’t a thing women did (or were welcomed to do).

Additionally, this person might be running on a decades-long plain-toast-and-coffee breakfast habit, with lower protein intake already ingrained before medication further reduced appetite.

The scale is dropping though, so they’re thrilled. It’s just that nobody’s measuring what kind of weight is dropping.

Keep in mind that this description is a starting hypothesis, not a diagnosis. Low activity and low protein raise the risk of muscle loss, but they don’t confirm it. That’s what the measures below are for.

Your job is to bring awareness to the invisible. Because once this person sees what’s at stake, they’ll be more likely to see the value in changing their habits, and in coaching.

However, theoretical warnings about muscle loss are easy to dismiss.

This is one of the reasons why Coach Kate says, “I don’t care if I coach you or not—please just get a DEXA as a baseline.”.

When a person has a quantifiable, objective measure of their muscle composition, it’s often more motivating than any amount of abstract concern.

Ideally, every person who begins a GLP-1 medication should get a DEXA scan before they start, then again at six or twelve months to see how they’re progressing.

If a client can’t or won’t do a DEXA, assess strength and function in other ways. Ask: “How do the stairs feel compared to a few months ago? What about carrying groceries?” Gather objective data too, recording baselines for squat, deadlift, and bench press (or other accessible exercises) to compare to over time. Declines in any of these areas can reveal potential muscle loss, and can motivate a client to take action.

Without protective strategies, up to 40 percent of weight lost from GLP-1 medications can come from lean mass, with a majority of that being muscle.2.

In order to prevent that from happening, there are two behaviors to prioritize:.

Industry observers note that ▶ Protein at every meal. When appetite is suppressed, every bite has to earn its place. Aim for 25-40 grams of protein at every meal and 15-20 grams for snacks. (On days when appetite is severely suppressed, protein powders can be a more palatable way to reach that target.).

In a recent development, ▶ Strength training, scaled to what they’d actually do. The term “weight lifting” might overwhelm a person who’s never set foot in a gym, so don’t start there. Start where PN always starts: Ask what they could do twice this week that they’re 9-out-of-10 confident they’d actually do. Sit-to-stands off the couch. A few moves with a resistance band. Bodyweight anything. Scale up from there, one week at a time.

This is the person for whom the medication has worked a little too well.

Their appetite hasn’t just decreased—it’s gone.

They’re not eating enough, and often don’t notice until you ask. “When did you last eat?” you say, and they say, “Ummm… Yesterday afternoon? I think?”.

Their protein and overall calorie intake is plummeting, and soon their energy levels will too.

Plus, something more subtle might also be happening: Food stops being a pleasure and becomes a chore, or even a source of dread.

Industry observers note that for some, this might seem like an upside down world. They may have spent their whole life fighting to eat less. The idea of fighting to eat more feels completely absurd—and entirely off their radar.

Before anything else: If there’s an active eating disorder in the picture, this medication likely shouldn’t have been prescribed. A vulnerability to disordered eating can both contribute to or be triggered by the above scenario.

In a recent development, so, scope of practice first. Ask this person if they’ve ever struggled with disordered eating. If the answer is yes, refer out to a doctor or a dietitian. You can absolutely stay involved as a guide, but not as the only professional in the room. Have your referral network ready before you need it.

Industry observers note that but sometimes, you won’t know. Your client may have been screened and cleared. Or, they may not have disclosed. So your job is to figure out what you’re actually looking at—and that starts with what Coach Toni calls the “show me” approach.

It has been revealed that as with every client here, treat this one as something to investigate, not a label. Rather than acting on a hunch, collect something concrete, such as a few days of food logging (in writing or via photos).

From there, it branches two ways.

▶ If they’ll track, do some food math, and the numbers may do the work for you. When some clients see that their calorie intake is hovering around 800 to 1,000 Calories per day, it’s the only wake up call they need. They weren’t intentionally restricting; they genuinely just had no idea.

For this client, establishing an eating routine is the best next action.

In a recent development, your client may be used to following appetite as a cue to eat, but now that medication has removed it, they need a different cue. That means eating on a schedule, likely every 3–4 hours, including protein at every one of those occasions. Portions can be small if appetite is very low, but they should be nutrient-dense.

▶ If they won’t track—and especially if they resist in a way that feels purposely avoidant—that resistance itself is information.

Coach Toni suggests that if you suspect that disordered eating is in the picture and a client is really resistant about tracking, it might be time for a crucial conversation—an often uncomfortable, but honest and essential conversation between a client and a coach.

She suggests leading with non-judgement and safety. For example:.

“I want you to know this is a safe space to talk. My goal as a coach is always to prioritize your overall health. However, there have been a couple of things you’ve shared recently that have me wondering whether we’re protecting your body’s basic needs.”.

Then name the specific things you noticed, sticking to facts. (“You’ve mentioned you’ve been losing hair and struggling more during workouts. Those can both be signs of undereating. Would you be open to revisiting food journaling for a short stretch so we can see more clearly what’s happening, or telling your doctor about your symptoms?”).

If this conversation is enough to help a client see the value in tracking, follow the advice after “If they’ll track” above.

If what surfaces is a genuinely troubled relationship with food, refer out, while offering to stay involved for support as needed.

This is the person who got the results they wanted with the medication, and is now choosing to wean off.

They’re not quitting because of crappy results or intolerable side effects, they’ve simply decided they don’t want to be on a GLP-1 forever.

The coaching opportunity here is, in part, about tempering expectations.

Most people imagine coming off as the finish line. Instead though, it’s more like starting a different endurance course: The medication has been managing their appetite, and now they have to.

In a recent development, ideally, you start working with this client while the medication is still doing some of the heavy lifting with appetite regulation. If you can have six months to build the right habits as well as prepare mentally for the tapering off period, your client will be in a much better position.

Make sure the previously mentioned habits—like resistance training and optimizing protein—are already firmly established. If your client is managing those habits consistently (not perfectly, but consistently), even on their busiest, most stressful, most side-effect-disrupted days, then they’re more likely to be able to maintain them when they’re off their medication and food distractions re-enter the picture.

After that, work on how you’ll continue to define success. This client has been accustomed to measuring it on the scale, but the scale will move—some regain is normal. So, ask them early: What does success look like if the scale ticks up eight pounds but your habits hold?

Be honest about the odds, too. People who changed nothing while on the medication almost universally regain most of the weight—usually within the first year and a half or so3—because the appetite that went down comes right back up.

However, people who integrate and sustain healthier nutrition and exercise behaviors while they’re on medication are four times better at maintaining a ten percent or higher weight loss when they come off the medication.4.

This is the person who was also getting great results on the medication—except instead of choosing to go off it on their own time, they’re forced to quit due to external circumstances.

Maybe their insurance stopped covering it, or they lost the job that came with the benefits, or the one drug they tolerated turned out to cost four times as much as the one they couldn’t tolerate.

About 50 percent of GLP-1 users stop the medication within the first year of using it.5 Some stop due to side effects, and others stop because they’ve gotten the results they want and they want to see if they can maintain them drug-free. But many are simply priced out. The latter is an especially frustrating scenario because, for this person, a “solution” exists. It’s just that, for them, the solution is out of reach.

Recent findings suggest that understandably, this person may be angry or even ashamed that they can’t afford this medication. Those feelings may or may not show up in your coaching, but it’s good to prepare for them anyway.

First, reassure this person that this is a system failure, not a personal one.

Whether someone can access affordable medication comes down to their insurance plan, the region they live in, and their socioeconomic status—also known as the social determinants of health. Those forces shape health outcomes far more than willpower does, and none of them are a measure of how hard someone has tried or how “worthy” they are.

Acknowledging that reality isn’t about throwing up your hands and saying, “Well, I’m screwed!” Rather, it’s about accepting some miserable truths about the world, and then shifting from self-blame to problem-solving.

Once they’ve had a chance to process some (very valid) anger and disappointment, it’s time to focus on what they can control.

At PN, we call this the Spheres of Control exercise. The image below indicates you how it works.

Access, price, and coverage are not on the list of controllables, and fighting those realities may only compound frustration.

Meanwhile, they can control other influential factors, like their protein intake, their training, their sleep, their food environment, and maybe their next insurance appeal.

Use the image above to begin a conversation with your client about what is within their control, and lean in hard on those factors.

Recent findings suggest that the truth is, you can’t predict how a client will respond to medication. And, some regain after stopping it is expected.

However, diet and lifestyle habits hugely affect what kind of weight clients lose, plus the rate and amount of that regain.

“I can’t promise anyone they’ll lose a specific amount of weight or that they’ll never regain it—and I’d be suspicious of any coach who did. What I can tell you is that the habits we build while the medication is doing its work are the ones that’ll still stand when it isn’t.”.

Of course, “coming off” isn’t the endpoint for everyone. Many providers now treat obesity as a chronic condition and these medications as long-term therapy—the same way we’d treat cardiac disease. Again, whether someone stays on, tapers, or stops is a conversation for them and their provider.

According to recent reports, but for those who do come off, Coach Toni states the people who hold their results share one thing: “They maintain consistency with their behaviors as if they were still on the medication. Like nothing changes.”.

She shares an analogy for why that works:.

In a recent development, “Think about the Oregon Trail. Wagon wheels made ruts in the trail by hitting the same ground over and over and over. You can still see those ruts today. Habits are the same way: If you lay down those neural pathways and reinforce them enough times while your client is on the medication, they’ll have a better chance of continuing on the same path even when they go off the medication.”.

It’s not: “You’ll keep it off.”.

It’s: “While the medication is doing its work, we’ll cut ruts deep enough that those pathways will still be there after the medication is gone.”.

Practically, that means regular resistance training, rock solid nutrition, appetite awareness, and attending to the parts of health that never show up on a scale—sleep, energy, mood, relationships, and identity, which is where Coach Toni lands:.

“Ideally, your client will have embraced the identity of a ‘latest person.’ As in, ‘I am the person who wakes up at 6 a.m. and walks two miles. I am the person who eats protein at every meal. I am the person who does resistance training because it builds the tissue I need to age well.’ That’s the client who maintains.”.

The seven client examples above help you answer two questions:.

Is this person ready for coaching?

How do I meet them where they are?

Once someone becomes your client, the question changes to:.

And when nausea, fatigue, stalled results, and weakening strength and physical function all show up at once in the same client, that can be tricky to answer.

Knowing where to start is one of the core skills taught in the upcoming GLP Coaching Institute Certification, developed in partnership with Precision Nutrition.

The certification combines GLP-1-specific science and practical coaching frameworks with PN’s proven coaching methodology. You’ll learn how to use a framework called The Five GLP-1 Types: Strength, Fuel, Fitness, Recovery, and Results.

According to recent reports, unlike the profiles in this article, the Five Types aren’t about how ready clients are. They’re coaching priorities: a way to decide what to work on first, and when to shift focus as a client’s needs change.

To learn more, join the waitlist. You’ll be the first to know when the certification debuts, with early access before enrolment opens to everyone else.

Bored With Your Workout? Try a Upcoming Level, Not a New Program

📅 25 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (529 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nerdfitness

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • This was the first thing a latest client said to me.
  • When we dug into it, here’s the pattern that emerged:.
  • Strength training, then running, then a yoga challenge, then back to lifting with a different app.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s the client story this comes from.

This was the first thing a latest client said to me.

When we dug into it, here’s the pattern that emerged:.

-> See something fresh, give that a try.

Strength training, then running, then a yoga challenge, then back to lifting with a different app.

Nerd Fitness Coaching was the latest in a long line of fresh starts.

And here’s the thing: all of it was GOOD.

Sources indicate that she was moving. She was trying latest things. She was having fun (at least at first).

But she was frustrated with herself.

She felt like she kept starting over and never getting anywhere.

And she wanted help figuring out what to do.

Let’s be real: trying something new is exciting.

It has been revealed that A newly introduced program, a new class, a new challenge. There’s a buzz to it.

And that buzz isn’t bad. Enjoying it is a big part of what keeps people moving.

The catch is that most goals need some repetition.

In a recent development, getting stronger, running farther, learning a skill. You get better at the things you practice again and again.

So the question isn’t “how do I stop getting bored?”.

It’s “how do I keep some of that new-thing fun AND repeat things enough to see progress?” 🧐.

That’s what we worked on together.

When I built her program, I kept its overall shape the same week to week.

But inside it, a few key exercises got a target. Something like:.

“Once you can do 12 reps with 25 pounds, we level up.”.

The targets were far enough away to stretch her, and close enough that she could hit them in 2 to 6 weeks of focused practice.

When she hit one, we leveled up that exercise: upcoming reps or weight, or a new variation. Everything else stayed put.

So something was always changing.

There was always a target she was closing in on and a level she’d recently beaten.

But the frame stayed the same. We were still working on the same overall qualities.

And that’s what let her progress stack up instead of resetting every few weeks.

She was able to stay really consistent with her program.

She still fell off some. (Life happens.).

But when she came back, she wasn’t looking for something new.

She was excited to pick up her program and keep progressing.

And sure, sometimes her goals would change.

We spent 6 months training for her first half marathon, then switched gears to focus on building muscle.

But that was a choice, not a restart.

If you love bouncing between things and you’re happy doing it, keep bouncing.

This is for when the bouncing starts to feel frustrating.

Before you reach for a fresh program, try a new level.

✅ Set a target you could reach in 2 to 6 weeks (a rep count or a weight).

✅ When you hit it, level up that one exercise with new reps, a new weight, or a new variation. Leave everything else alone.

According to recent reports, I’m excited to see what you come up with. 😃.

#80198. I Got Shingles Training for a Marathon. I’m Not the Only One.

I Got Shingles Training for a Marathon. I’m Not the Only One.

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1531 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Triathlete

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Shingles typically appears as a band of blistering, painful rash on one side of the body.
  • I had just finished the last hard training run of my marathon build, 19 miles with 15 at race pace.
  • “You’ll have two weeks to taper, and you’ll be ready to run that BQ (Boston Marathon Qualifying time) on race day.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Shingles typically appears as a band of blistering, painful rash on one side of the body. (Photo: Getty Images).

I had just finished the last hard training run of my marathon build, 19 miles with 15 at race pace. I nailed it, but couldn’t help thinking it felt harder than it should have.

“It’s just nerves,” I told myself. “You’ll have two weeks to taper, and you’ll be ready to run that BQ (Boston Marathon Qualifying time) on race day.”.

Industry observers note that the next day, I felt exhausted, and my ribs were sore and tender to the touch. I started to wonder if I’d pulled a muscle in my rib cage while breathing heavily during my training run. I, of course, turned to Google. “Ribs sore from running.” “Ribs hurt after running.” Most of the posts advised that I’d feel better in a day.

It has been revealed that but I didn’t feel better the next day. Instead, I noticed a small pink mark on my stomach, and now my ribs felt both sore and tingly. My Google searches grew more alarming: I could have shingles.

In a recent development, I scheduled an appointment for that same day, and my doctor confirmed it. She took one look at me and stated, “I’m so sorry, you have shingles.”.

Recent findings suggest that shingles is a painful viral infection that looks like a terrible rash and usually involves nerve pain that can last for months. The virus comes from dormant chickenpox in your body that can reappear when you’re stressed.

In a recent development, my doctor asked about stressors in my life. “I haven’t really been that stressed,” I promised, saying my family life and my career were extremely smooth. “But I have been training for a marathon,” I mentioned.

“That could do it,” she told me. “Your body is clearly telling you that you were pushing too hard.”.

In a recent development, I’m 43, younger than the typical shingles patient, but I’m part of an unfortunate trend. Shingles cases are on the rise and the biggest increase is among people in their 30s and 40s. One study found overall shingles cases nearly doubled between 2005 and 2021. Another found cases in Americans under 50 quadrupled from the late 1940s to 2000, and are still going up, according to data from the CDC.

A massive reason for the increase among millennials is that we fall into a gap: 50 and up, and you can get the shingles vaccine; 30 and under, and you’ve had the chickenpox vaccine, which will make getting shingles way less likely.

That age range is also most common among marathoners, so my substantial question was whether running, especially hard training, can give you shingles. Unfortunately, that specific question hasn’t been extensively studied, so there’s no clear-cut answer. But doctors are drawing correlations between heavy training and whether it decreases the body’s immunity overall.

There’s research that shows immunity dips after heavy training, indicates David Nieman, DrPH, FACSM, director of the Human Performance Laboratory at Appalachian State University. He pointed to a study involving mice and the herpes virus.

In a recent development, “When you infected the mice and then forced them to run to exhaustion, there was a higher mortality rate in those mice than mice that just did moderate activity and rested,” he says. “Moderate activity actually helped a little bit, but by far the really bad response was in the mice that ran to exhaustion.”.

In a recent development, in another study, researchers gave horses the flu and then ran them really hard. Those horses developed a longer-lasting, more intense bout of the flu compared to the horses who were infected but didn’t run hard, he said.

But Nieman and other researchers agree that moderate exercise can actually boost your immunity. James Turner, a professor at the Sport, Exercise and Rehabilitation Sciences school at the University of Birmingham, claims it’s far more common that inadequate sleep, diet and psychological stress suppress immunity than exercise, even really hard training.

“Research on both prolonged exercise and marathon running shows that antibody responses are not suppressed and might actually be higher,” he says.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, Dr. William Schaffner, MD, a professor of infectious diseases at Vanderbilt Health who’s an expert in shingles, claims it’s too soon to say definitely that lots of stress leads to the virus. He points out there’s no evidence that soldiers in combat or police and firefighters have an increased risk of shingles.

Industry observers note that “When people get a shingles episode, there is a tendency to look back in their lives to see if there might be some sort of inciting event or stressful event and there’s a tendency to link the two,” he says. “But the question is, is that just coincidence because there’s a lot of stress in life, or was it a causal relationship? I think we’ll still have to say that hasn’t been definitively settled.”.

It has been revealed that instead, for Schaffner, the likeliest explanation for the increase in shingles is because the chickenpox vaccine is decreasing our exposure to chickenpox. We used to all get chickenpox as children, and so the virus was more common in the wild. That gave our immune systems a boost. Now that there’s a vaccine, that isn’t happening, which means we may be more likely to get shingles, he said.

Whether my running caused my shingles or not, as soon as I had my diagnosis, my next questions were about my marathon. My doctor said my symptoms would likely peak in four days to a week, and so it still seemed possible I would be ready for race day. I rushed out to get a seven-day course of Valtrex—if you start an antiviral treatment swiftly enough, it can stop the spread of the shingles rash.

Sources indicate that but as the week passed and the rash grew along my rib cage to my back, it only continued to feel worse. I was achy everywhere, and my ribs felt like they were constantly being stabbed with tiny needles. A week later, I called it and canceled my marathon plans, harboring a hope that within a few weeks I would be better and could rebound to run my BQ.

Industry observers note that what I did next probably hurt my cause rather than helped it. As soon as I felt a bit better, I would go out and do a race-pace run, which would give me a painful setback that lasted for several days. This likely was making my bout with the virus longer, Nieman says.

He reminded me of the mice who were running to exhaustion and not getting well. The mice really needed to keep it low-key to get an immune boost, not drain.

“If they did 30 minutes of something like a brisk walk equivalent, that would help a little bit,” he says.

My conversation with him sounded like a negotiation.

“I’m mostly feeling better, but I still sometimes have sensations in my ribs, so do I still need to take it easy?” I asked.

“I have a lot of empathy. I know you don’t want to hear it,” he remarked gently. Nieman has run 58 marathons himself, so he knows the feeling. “You don’t want anybody telling you not to run, but this is where you’ve got to be really, really careful and just bide your time and slowly get back into it once you feel better.”.

Recent findings suggest that his advice to runners: listen to your body and don’t push yourself. That’s not an easy metric for marathoners who are used to pushing beyond what feels comfortable, but Nieman claims exhaustion can exacerbate the nerve pain and make it all last much longer.

Other things to keep in mind: it’s possible that sunburns can impede your immune system, so cover up once you’re back out and running, states Jennifer Moffat, a SUNY microbiology and immunology professor and expert on chickenpox and shingles.

According to recent reports, and, Moffat claims, while you still have a rash, you’re contagious and can spread the virus to others through contact. If you’re at the gym or anywhere you might touch other people, you should have the rash fully covered.

She also advises keeping an eye on the other stresses around marathons, like not eating enough, not sleeping enough, and the mental stress around races.

“The anticipation, logistics, travel hassles, changes in environment and food, rivalries with other competitors, jet lag, time away from family, the cost can become overwhelming,” she claims. “Getting to the starting line of a marathon is much more than showing up with your shoes tied.”.

In fact, she notes, it’s common for people to come down with other viral infections right before a race (the dreaded taper cold).

Sources indicate that as for me, two months after my rash first appeared, I finally truly threw in the towel. I couldn’t keep up any kind of marathon training without making myself feel worse, so I switched to low-effort maintenance running and decided my BQ would have to come next year.

#80197. The beliefs these Master Health Coaches had to unlearn (and you might too)

📅 28 Aug 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (3063 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Precisionnutrition ↗ Open Full Page

The beliefs these Master Health Coaches had to unlearn (and you might too)

📅 28 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3063 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Precisionnutrition

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For example, in Motivational Interviewing, an effective communication style used in coaching and counseling, there is something called the “righting reflex.”.
  • The righting reflex is the instinct to help or “fix” a client, as well as give them directions on how best to change.
  • Sounds like a great instinct to follow if you’re a coach, right?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For example, in Motivational Interviewing, an effective communication style used in coaching and counseling, there is something called the “righting reflex.”.

The righting reflex is the instinct to help or “fix” a client, as well as give them directions on how best to change. Often, the righting reflex is particularly strong in people who really, really care.

Sounds like a great instinct to follow if you’re a coach, right?

We are now entering upside-down-land.

Motivational Interviewing describes how this (beautiful, well-intentioned) instinct to help can actually hinder a client’s progress.

That’s because when we swoop in to fix, correct, or steer, clients often do the exact opposite of what we’re hoping for: They dig in and get defensive.

Recent findings suggest that push someone the “right” way and, paradoxically, they’ll start advocating for the very habits they came to you to change. You end up being the one arguing for change—which leaves them to argue against it. Everyone walks away a little more frustrated, and the client feels more stuck than ever.

According to recent reports, instead, great, experienced coaches learn to get curious instead of corrective. (They might even encourage the client to explore not changing!).

It has been revealed that that’s just one example of an upside-down skill that separates a good coach from a masterful one. But it’s certainly not the only example.

We asked some of Precision Nutrition’s most seasoned PN Level 2 Master Health Coach Certified coaches a simple question:.

What’s something you were sure about early in your career that you later had to unlearn?

Their (honest, and sometimes humbling) answers are below, plus the wiser way forward they adopted, and are now sharing with you.

Our first lesson to unlearn comes from PN in-house coach Jeremy Fernandes, PN2-MHC.

With over 14 years of coaching experience, Coach Jeremy is known for his friendly, comfortable, “talk to me like I’m your buddy” coaching style. Which is ironic, because as you’ll see, he started off his career leaning heavily on a rigid structure that was actually pushing clients away.

Here’s what Coach Jeremy has to say:.

At the beginning of my career, when I’d been a personal trainer for a year or two, I had a friend ask if I offered nutrition coaching. And my first move was: Here are all of the forms. And when I say “all of the forms,” I mean all of them—I probably sent this person 20 pages to fill out.

Three weeks later I had to hunt them down, and we ended up filling them out together—which took two and a half grueling hours.

If not for those forms, we could have started actually coaching, like, 20 days earlier.

Not long after, another friend showed up at my door with this white-hot intensity: “Tell me what to do, I’m ready,” they noted. And I immediately dumped a metaphorical bucket of ice water on them with those darn forms. It was radio silence after that.

The problem was that I was operating like my sole job was to extract information from a person and then solve the mystery—as if I had some advanced pattern recognition about you that you didn’t have about yourself.

And unfortunately, I kept on that terrible path for a while.

What finally prompted a change was going through the Level 2 Master Health Coaching Certification.

Going through that course, I saw there was a better framework—one that doesn’t rely on me robotically extracting information.

Recent findings suggest that I learned to let the client take the lead, and then just listen and maybe ask a few good questions. And it works so much better—for everyone.

In a recent development, now I work from the assumption that my client knows themselves better than anyone. One of my most valuable questions is simply:.

“What have you tried before, what did you like about it, and what didn’t you like?”.

When I let people take the floor, they nail the really big stuff more often than not—in a way my paperwork and my detective work never facilitated.

Honestly, the forms were me projecting professionalism, because back then I didn’t feel like a professional. My identity as a coach never felt natural until after L2. Now, just letting someone talk feels like coaching. We start with a connection, and then I just let them fill in the gaps.

The next lesson to unlearn comes from PN Director of Community Engagement and in-house coach Kate Solovieva, PN2-MHC.

With over 16 years of coaching experience, Coach Kate is known for her honesty and incisiveness. She has a way of dropping realness on her clients that may first feel like a shock, but ultimately ends up getting her clients to the heart of the matter much faster. But one hard truth she had to face was her own.

Here’s what Coach Kate has to say:.

You know the story: You reach the healthy weight, the habits lock in, and the weight just stays stable on its own. You hit “save” and move on with your happily ever after.

And that is not the case at all.

At least most of the time. It’s true, some goals really are like that. If you want to run a marathon, you can pick a race date, follow a training program, show up to the start line, run it—and then you never have to run again and you will still have achieved that goal. That’s a real destination; you cross the finish line once and check the goal off.

It has been revealed that but weight loss, muscle gain, body recomposition, building a habit of movement or eating well—those aren’t like that. Especially when the goal means working against a chronic tendency, like a predisposition to high blood pressure, or to hating exercise, or to living in a larger body than you’d prefer.

Those goals come with a pretty good amount of ongoing and intentional maintenance—daily, weekly, monthly. There’s no save button.

In a recent development, this realization didn’t come from one single client or one moment for me. It came through a collection of observations, including observations of myself. But once I saw it, it changed how I coach.

According to recent reports, I realized that if there’s no real finish line, then my job is to manufacture finish lines along the way. That way, my clients continually feel like they’re accomplishing something satisfying.

I take the big goal and break it into something specific and daily—and then I insert smaller outcome goals into the journey.

Recent findings suggest that for instance, someone going from sedentary to wanting to lose 100 pounds is facing a huge goal, full of behaviors and identities they’ll have to grow into. So along the way, we might set a goal of running a single mile without stopping. Strictly speaking, that doesn’t have much to do with the bigger goal—but it also has everything to do with it. It’s checkable. Achievable. Ideally it’s also something they’re a little excited about: fun, interesting, maybe even a little scary, but still within reach.

Because here’s the thing: It’s very hard to motivate the human brain to work out three times a week for the rest of their life to “get healthier.” “Being healthy” isn’t tangible, it’s not immediate—you can’t feel that far-off outcome in your body.

But striving towards a fun, achievable goal in the next three to six months? That’s real. It also builds in structure, and provides those little spikes of motivation—the hit of dopamine you get from working hard at something and actually accomplishing it.

Health isn’t something we ever fully “accomplish” or check off. So we have to give ourselves these little concrete goals along the way that we can feel and see and be delighted by.

The next lesson to unlearn comes from PN content creator Azul Corajoria, CPT, PN2-MHC.

With over nine years of coaching experience, Coach Azul’s coaching fingerprint is empathetic, relatable, and endlessly encouraging.

While these traits always came naturally to her, for a long time, she thought she had to adopt an opposite style to help certain clients (and herself) to “get back in line” when habits didn’t go as planned.

Here’s what Coach Azul has to say:.

Early in my coaching career, I thought that if someone wasn’t following through on what they said they would do, it’s because they needed more structure or just to get their “head in the game.”.

I couldn’t understand why someone would invest in coaching and then not do the things we planned.

It was especially confusing because most of my clients had “discipline.” They were successful, responsible, hardworking people who revealed up for their jobs, families, and everyone else in their lives.

Meanwhile, I was also “disciplined” in many areas of my life—yet I also struggled with eating well and exercising consistently.

At this time, I felt this lack of consistency was my fault, and went straight to being really angry at myself. I thought I was just missing the “perfect something” (the perfect workout, the perfect diet) to help me change, so I’d just move from thing to thing, but each one would bring fresh disappointment.

I was incredibly frustrated by this cycle, and my response was to get stricter and harsher with myself.

It’s hard to say when it all changed. It wasn’t an overnight epiphany; it was a culmination of years of getting curious, being open to different methods, like the Body Positivity Movement and Intuitive Eating. I dove into self-compassion and positive psychology research, and I went through the PN Level 2 Master Health Coaching Certification.

I applied everything I learned, and I noticed that the more open and curious I was, the better my clients responded. Slowly, that turned into the realization that the more open and curious I was with myself, the better I would respond.

I stopped binge eating. I started enjoying exercise more. I took more career risks.

Industry observers note that I learned that when we can respond to a setback with curiosity instead of punishment, we’re much more likely to stay engaged. When I allow myself to be disappointed by an action, take responsibility for it, and remain on my own side, I feel safer reflecting and taking risks. The more I do that, the more likely I am to achieve the things I want.

Sometimes the most helpful thing we can teach a client (and ourselves) is not how to push harder or “just be more disciplined.” It’s how to make a mistake, remain on our own side, and keep going.

It has been revealed that because self-compassion is not the opposite of accountability; it’s often what makes accountability possible. (I call it “compassionate accountability.”).

None of us will ever be the “perfect” coach, and we don’t have to be. The more human I’ve allowed myself to be, the better relationships I’ve had with my clients. My biggest goal as a coach is to create an environment my client feels safe to come back to with not only their wins, but their losses. The safer they feel being honest and open with me, the safer they’ll feel to try new things—and over time they’ll build the confidence to do it themselves.

The next lesson to unlearn comes from PN in-house coach and Level 2 Master Health Coaching Certification instructor Dom Matteo, PN2-MHC, NBC-HWC.

With over 16 years of coaching experience, Coach Dom stands out for his non-judgemental attitude and excellent listening skills. For Dom, these traits are relatively inherent, but they’ve also been carefully developed and honed, in part by letting go of what he calls the “coach’s ego”—the assumption that he already knew what a client’s success should look like, and that he was the one who got to keep score.

Here’s what Coach Dom has to say:.

I took that stated goal at face value, and treated whatever number they gave me as the measuring stick, as the most important thing to work towards.

But then, I’d see a client struggling to do their actions even 50 percent of the time, and I’d think: ‘This person is never going to be happy, because this won’t get them to the goal weight they told me they wanted.’.

Remember, I assumed the number was the real goal.

However, again and again, those same clients would turn out to be genuinely happy with their progress, not because they hit their exact goal, but because they felt so much better about themselves and their lives.

What I learned is that the stated outcome was almost never the true goal for many of them. When they mentioned ‘lose 50 pounds,’ what they really meant was: I want to feel better. And being consistent even half the time, over a year, netted results they were thrilled with. Because they felt better. They felt different.

So the thing I had to let go of was my own scorecard. Who am I to tell a client that what they’re doing isn’t good enough, if they’re happy with how things are going?

My new definition of progress became less about approaching a specific final number and more about another question: “Am I a little better today than I was yesterday?”.

These days, I spend time up front helping a client build what we call a “wellness vision.” We clarify their values, and what success actually looks and feels like to them.

Then, instead of assuming I know how to measure their progress, I’ll ask: “How will you know if this is helping? How do you want to measure success?”.

In a recent development, the result is that even a client who’s fixated on the scale can see other signs of progress long before the scale actually changes. And often, those other signs are the things they really wanted to change in the first place.

In a recent development, it turns out the most useful thing I can provide isn’t a judgement about whether a client is succeeding. Instead, it’s to help them determine and notice their own success, by their own measures.

The next lesson to unlearn comes from PN in-house coach and Level 2 Master Health Coaching Certification instructor Jason Bonn, PN2-MHC, NBC-HWC.

According to recent reports, with over 18 years of coaching experience, Coach Jason’s clients describe him as patient, observant, and deeply dedicated. He has a knack for spotting a client’s potential—though as you’ll read in this story, Coach Jason learned that getting too focused on a specific version of that potential sometimes kept him from seeing other ways his clients could grow and thrive.

Here’s what Coach Jason has to say:.

For me, progress felt like a puzzle to solve: I’d play with adjustments to exercise volume or intensity, calorie or protein intake, eating more slowly, eating to 80 percent fullness, all the fundamental stuff.

But then, because of one client I still think about, I began to shift how I thought about “progress.”.

He was in our PN coaching program. He lost 40 to 50 pounds in his first six months—which was great—but then everything stalled.

We tried adjustment after adjustment for the next two and a half years. We added more protein, more cardio, and worked through his particular peccadillo, eating corn chips at night. But none of it moved his numbers.

What got me was that he kept showing up anyway: three straight years, re-enrolling each time, even though the scale had plateaued.

That told me something was working for him—it just wasn’t something I recognized yet.

In his third year, we stopped looking only at the gym and his diet, and started looking at his whole life. He was a landscape painter, so we built his practices around that instead: make a sketch or work on a painting daily, anything that sparked some joy or interest. Within a couple of weeks, he was getting on his bike and riding out to further places for different scenery to paint.

In part because of this client, I’m now a lot more cognizant of coaching the whole person, and considering their Deep Health. Weight and performance numbers are just one piece of a much bigger picture that includes relationships, emotional wellbeing, and what someone finds meaningful.

I’ve also stopped zeroing in on “problem” behavior.

I try to understand a person’s life overall—not just the behavior I’ve been hired to help with—because there’s a connectedness to it all, and behavior tends to emerge within the context of someone’s life.

I’ve also stopped treating the coaching relationship as a means to an outcome and started treating it as the main thing—the sun that everything orbits, the glue that holds it all together.

Industry observers note that that client kept coming back for three years because the relationship mattered to him. By the end, I’d stopped thinking I was failing him. The weight loss was such a small part of the success. The relationship was the bigger piece.

Coaching mastery isn’t about stockpiling more information. (Your clients can Google information or ask a chatbot, and so can you.).

It’s about developing the judgment to know when to use what you know, when to set it aside, and when the most helpful thing you can do is nothing at all, except be there.

But that kind of judgment is hard to build alone; it takes practice, expert feedback, and a few humbling moments with real clients—which is exactly what the PN Level 2 Master Health Coach Certification is designed to offer.

With enough practice, self-awareness, and the right training, you can gain the wisdom and skill of the above coaches.

But the best coaches, it turns out, are defined less by what they know than by what they’ve been willing to unlearn.

Ready to move from competent to truly masterful—in 20 weeks?

The PN Level 2 Master Health Coaching Certification is an advanced, practice-based program designed for coaches who want to work at a deeper level—and do it sooner than the traditional 5–10 year path.

One Bike for Everything? Our Editors Tested Hybrid Bikes for Daily Riding—These 10 Picks Are Best for Commuting, Fitness, and Light Trails

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Sources indicate that when I worked in bike shops, we sold tons of hybrid bikes.
  • Outside of cycling circles, the term “hybrid” often refers to vehicles that pair an electric motor with an internal combustion engine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Sources indicate that when I worked in bike shops, we sold tons of hybrid bikes. These bicycles are ideal for riders who say, “I need a bike that does a little of everything.” If you’re seeking versatility, a hybrid is often your best bike option. They’re a good choice for general fitness, commuting, running errands, and family rides.

Outside of cycling circles, the term “hybrid” often refers to vehicles that pair an electric motor with an internal combustion engine. However, in bike-speak, hybrids are a bicycle style that combines elements of road bikes and mountain bikes. Hybrids range from lightweight, sporty bikes designed for roads and bike paths to more rugged models suitable for light off-road use.

While they’re not ideal for die-hard mountain bikers or roadies seeking speed and the highest performance, hybrids work surprisingly well for many people on real-world rides. Typically, hybrids blend the lightweight frame, fast-rolling tires, and larger gears of road bikes with flat handlebars and the upright riding position of hardtail mountain bikes. Some hybrid models also feature suspension forks similar to those used on bikes designed for more aggressive, technical trails.

It has been revealed that the Cannondale Quick 3 is our overall favorite hybrid for its fast feel and smooth ride, comfortable upright riding position, and reasonable price. These qualities make it great for upcoming riders who may be hesitant about incorporating regular bike riding into their routine.

The Quick 3 features a comfortable Selle Royal saddle and Ergon grips. It also has mounts for adding a rear rack (the fork lacks rack mounts, however) and fenders to keep road spray out of your eyes and off your backside. While the pricier Quick 2 features a carbon fork and 1x9 Shimano drivetrain, the Quick 3 uses a steel fork and 1x8-speed Shimano system. These differences add a little weight, but the bike still has the gear range to tackle the hills on your commute or rides.

Industry observers note that cannondale also offers the Quick 3 with a step-through frame. It also sells the Quick CX 3 model with a suspension fork.

BUY QUICK 3 STEP-THROUGH - $749 BUY QUICK CX 3 - $849.

The CTY 1.1 (by REI’s Co-op Cycles house brand) is a capable, affordable hybrid. The CTY is a great choice for a wide range of riders—especially for budget-minded beginners and commuters. The bike has an upright riding position (versus the sporty fit of fitness-focused hybrids). This geometry, along with a comfortable memory foam saddle and gel grips, makes the CTY 1.1 more comfortable than many competitors.

Commuters will appreciate the CTY’s flat-resistant, wire-bead 40mm tires with reflective sidewalls; they let you roll over potholes, dirt, gravel, random road debris, and even the occasional curb. For all-weather stopping power, REI equips the bike with Tektro mechanical disc brakes, and the Shimano 3x8-speed drivetrain gives you enough gear range to get you most anywhere you want to go.

BUY CTY 1.1 STEP-THROUGH - $649 $519.

Based in Brooklyn’s Greenpoint neighborhood, Brooklyn Bike Co. uses firsthand knowledge to design well-priced bikes that can withstand the rigors of NYC commutes—and the brand’s Roebling model is a great example. While the Roebling’s design is simple and understated, it’s entirely practical for commuting, fitness, and leisurely rides.

Brooklyn builds the Roebling around a double-butted cromoly frame. Although its skinny tubes look retro compared to the shaped, formed ones used on alloy-framed hybrids, the bike is lightweight (approximately 30 pounds), durable, and easy to ride. The Roebling features a 1x9-speed drivetrain with an 11-41-tooth cassette and 42T chainring. This gives you an easy gear for hills and a significant enough gear for speed on flatter parts of your ride. Unlike many similarly priced hybrids, the Roebling uses V-style rim brakes. While not as flashy as disc brakes, V-brakes are lighterweight and easier to adjust.

If you’re 5’6” or shorter, also check out the Lorimer. It’s essentially the same bike as the Roebling, but in smaller sizes (and in two color options).

According to recent reports, want the easiest-to-maintain, rust-proof hybrid for commuting and riding around town? Then, Priority’s Eight hybrid is probably the best choice you can find. Weighing only 27 pounds, the Eight is lighter than many hybrids thanks to its aluminum frame and carbon fiber fork.

Industry observers note that priority originally introduced its iconic Eight commuter bike in 2016 but discontinued it after a few years. However, the New York City-based brand relaunched the model due to rider demand—and it’s a winner. The Eight features a Gates Carbon belt drive drivetrain instead of a standard chain; this system requires no lube or maintenance (other than an occasional wipe-down with a rag). For gearing to scale hills and overpasses, Priority equips the Eight with an eight-speed (hence its name) Shimano Alfine internally geared rear hub with a 307% gear range.

The Eight comes in traditional and step-through style frames. For all-weather commuters, Priority also offers the Continuum Onyx. It has fenders and dynamo lights that never need charging. Plus, it uses the Enviolo CVT (continuously variable transmission) rear hub. It has the same gear range as a traditional 21-speed drivetrain.

It has been revealed that test team member Tom Messina often rides the Cannondale Quick 2 for his daily commutes and on the local rail trail. He’s ridden it through snow squalls and on beautiful fall afternoons, and he’s impressed with the bike’s performance, versatility, and overall value.

“At $949, you’ll be pressed to find many better options on a commuter or introduction bike than this one, especially from a brand I trust as much as Cannondale,” he noted. Messina particularly likes the bike’s low weight, wide-range Shimano Cues 9-speed drivetrain, and sure-stopping hydraulic disc brakes. “It’s a top-tier bike for those getting back into riding after a long time off, or spinning the bike path on a sunny day.”.

According to recent reports, want a suspension fork? Cannondale also offers the Quick CX 2 for $1,099.

It has been revealed that most hybrids use a road-style frame with a mix of mountain bike and pavement components. Scott takes a slightly different approach with its Scale Gravel series; the result is a blend of mountain bike and gravel tech ideal for adventure riding, backpacking, and commutes in foul weather or worn-out roads.

Intended “to go the distance over any and all types of terrain,” this adventure-ready variant of Scott’s Scale XC racing hardtail features an aluminum frame and carbon fork with multiple attachment points for carrying gear. The Gravel 20 has a SRAM Eagle 70 1x12 drivetrain that provides extremely low gearing, and Shimano hydraulic disc brakes ensure strong stopping power.

Industry observers note that while the Gravel 20 is probably way too much bike for most people’s rides, it’s a perfect option if your gravel roads and rides are more extreme than most. However, if you like the look of this bike and want a lighterweight option, Scott offers a range of Scale Gravel models—some with carbon frames and electronic shifting—from $1,700 to $5,500.

In a recent development, this FX 2 earns high marks for its value. Its aluminum frame and fork have a look and feel of some of Trek’s more premium hybrids, without the added price. Internal cable routing keeps the frame looking clean, and like its electrified counterpart, it comes equipped with a Shimano Cues 1x9 drivetrain and Tektro hydraulic disc brakes. At just 26 pounds, it’s impressively light for a bike this capable. Keep the FX 2 as-is for a sleek, fast look, or use the rack and fender mounts for added utility.

Sources indicate that if you want substantial tires for soaking up rough terrain, this isn’t the bike for you. The FX 2 rolls on 35mm tires with a max clearance of 40mm, making it better suited for smooth roads and cinder trails. But if you like a fast, efficient ride, this is a great bike at a great price.

Even though hybrids typically blend road and mountain bike technology and features, many hybrids are biased towards riding pavement and gravel roads rather than trails. However, Polygon’s Heist 2 leans more heavily on its mountain bike DNA.

In a recent development, the Heist’s frame styling closely resembles hardtail mountain bikes, and its geometry isn’t too far from XC racing hardtails from only a decade ago. With a 63mm travel SR Suntour NEX fork and 1x8 Shimano Alivio/Essa drivetrain, you can take the Heist on light-duty singletrack. (Though you might want tires knobbier than the stock WTB Riddlers if you have anything but smooth trails.).

Industry observers note that specialized has sold its Sirrus platform for decades, and that experience shows in this bike’s details. This bike embodies the “I need it to do everything” ethos.

It has been revealed that the Sirrus features sporty geometry for a fast ride feel and a rigid fork to save some weight. Specialized equips the Sirrus X 2.0 with a wide-range Shimano Cues 9-speed drivetrain, hydraulic disc brakes, and 40mm semi-slick tires for some off-pavement use. The Sirrus frame also has mounts for racks (for commuting or touring) and fenders.

BUY SIRRUS X 2.0 STEP-THROUGH - $850.

Many “women’s hybrids” use step-through frames, or are men’s bikes in a different color. As one of cycling’s only brands focused exclusively on women riders, Liv designs its frame geometries and touchpoints (such as saddles and grips) to better fit women’s bodies.

Alight is Liv’s hybrid platform; Alight models feature flat handlebars, rigid forks, 700x38c tires, and an upright riding position. This makes the Alight comfortable and stable without compromising too much speed. You can use the Alight for fitness rides and commutes since Liv equips the bike with mounts for a rack and fenders.

The Alight Disc 2 features a 1x9 MicroShift drivetrain, with an 11-46 tooth cassette and 40T chainring. This gives the Alight a low gear for climbing hills; however, some riders may find the gearing isn’t hard enough for flat sections of road.

Sources indicate that most hybrid models are traditional human-powered bicycles. However, some brands offer hybrid-style electric bikes. These hybrids feature lightweight electric motors and rechargeable batteries to provide pedal assistance up to 20 or 28 mph, depending on local regulations.

Below are two electric-assist hybrid bikes we’ve tested and recommend. For more e-bike options, check out our in-depth Electric Bike Buyer’s Guide.

Sources indicate that this relatively affordable seven-speed model from Aventon delivers simplicity and style that is tough to beat—and now even more so with hydraulic disc brakes on this revamped version. Push the throttle, and the Soltera’s brushless hub motor kicks in, assisting you more gently as you begin pedaling.

The Soltera features disc brakes, an integrated light, and turn signals. The battery is hidden in the bike’s frame (a surprising feature compared to the bolt-on vibe of many bikes in this price range), which helps the bike blend in with non-electric bikes. Best for smoother roads and bike paths, the Soltera delivers the essential features a city rider needs in a 46-pound package.

In a recent development, many electric bikes exceed 60 or 80 pounds, so a sub-40-pound e-bike is rather impressive. Unfortunately, e-bikes this light are usually rather expensive. However, Velotric’s Tempo only costs $1,499 and boasts a 39 lb. (claimed) weight. Velotric achieves this weight reduction and low cost by ditching the bulky suspension fork and using a smaller battery.

Like most hybrids, and unlike many e-bikes, the Tempo features 700c gravel tires. These tires roll quicker than 26- or 27.5-inch tires on pavement while giving the Tempo improved traction on dirt roads and gravel paths. Velotric offers the Tempo in a traditional double diamond frame and a mid-step design. Both frames are available in two colors and two sizes.

Since riders use hybrids in different ways, brands make various styles of these bikes to meet their needs and budgets. Some focus on lightweight and speed, while others are more rugged and can even tackle some easier mountain bike trails. There are also hybrids with features such as racks, fenders, and lights for commuting and touring, as well as some e-bike models.

When shopping for a hybrid, I recommend first thinking about where you will ride it most often. If you will mostly ride on paved roads and bike paths, consider a hybrid that focuses on low weight and has slick tires. If you’re commuting, look for bikes with mounts for racks or fenders, and have heavy-duty tires and wheels. For gravel paths or light-duty trail riding, consider hybrid models with suspension forks and knobbier tires.

Industry observers note that lastly, I always remind hybrid shoppers to consider a bike’s long-term use. Look for hybrids that use common, universal-sized components and avoid those with proprietary features or gimmicks. Riders often own their hybrids for several years, sometimes decades. You’ll want to be able to service and repair the bike down the line, especially if you use it for commuting.

In a recent development, as Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and Upcoming England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recently, I asked you: where are you feeling most stuck with your fitness right now?

In a recent development, hundreds of you wrote back. Thoughtful, honest answers. Thank you.

I’m working my way through all of them.

And one theme jumped out at me IMMEDIATELY.

One reader, let’s call her Supergirl, said it this way:.

If you’ve ever had a great run (for a few days or a few years) and then couldn’t find your way back, this one’s for you, too.

In a recent development, I’ve heard this so many times in my coaching career. You were in a really good groove. Something knocked you off. And getting back on track feels incredibly difficult, and you don’t know why.

According to recent reports, I’ve experienced this myself! I was in a groove with food logging. It felt easy. Then I took a break, and when I tried to start up again, I couldn’t get it going with any consistency for the life of me.

Here’s my take after nearly two decades of coaching: I doubt this is a motivation thing.

You were cruising at 70 miles an hour. You made a pit stop, and now you’re trying to jump the car straight back to 70. Instantly.

Of course that’s going to feel rough!

Another reader put it really well in their message to me:.

According to recent reports, that’s driving with your eyes on the rearview mirror. And it makes anything smaller feel like it doesn’t count.

But smaller is how you get back up to speed.

According to recent reports, after multiple false starts with food logging, I realized I was falling into the same trap. And instead of forcing myself to weigh and measure anything, I gave myself a different on-ramp. Protein and veggies at each meal? Check. That allowed me to build back up again and find the groove that worked for me in this current phase of life.

Previous success can feel like a scorecard that you have to grade yourself against.

But what worked before might not work for you right now.

And it’s notable to remember that most of us needed an on-ramp the first time, too. That part didn’t change after some time off.

Sources indicate that you know what you “should” be doing. Let’s put that aside for now.

Instead, let’s shrink down what our focus is. We don’t have to figure out the whole routine. Not the whole week. Let’s work on today.

Try this thought experiment with me: if you didn’t have any expectations of what this “should” look like, what is one thing that feels doable today?

Maybe it’s performing your warm-up routine. Or doing the first round of exercises in your workout.

Maybe it’s batch cooking some protein tonight, or running to the grocery store to stock up on some easy fruit and veggie options.

Industry observers note that try it out, and see how that feels. Is the resistance still there? If it isn’t, you’ve found the start of your on-ramp. 🙌.

According to recent reports, and if it still feels hard to start? That’s OK, too. We can choose a different entry point and try again.

It has been revealed that if you’re in that camp of “I know what to do. I can’t get myself to start,” give yourself a different, smaller on-ramp.

Your on-ramp doesn’t have to be forever.

But it may be exactly what you need right now.

Hit reply and let me know what yours looks like.

## The Moment You Recline Into ANA "The Room" The flight attendant slides your suite door closed. You're somewhere over the Pacific, 35,000 feet above the ocean, enclosed in what ANA calls "The Room" — a fully private, floor-to-ceiling enclosed business class suite on a Boeing 777-300ER. The seat converts to a fully flat 78-inch bed. There's direct aisle access. The service is famously meticulous. And you're flying from New York to Tokyo in a product that rivals first class on most other carriers. This is not a fantasy. This is what 90,000 Virgin Atlantic Flying Club miles buys you on ANA's JFK → NRT route. ### The Math That Should Stop You Cold A one-way business class ticket on ANA between New York and Tokyo typically retails for **$6,000 to $12,000 in cash**. That's not a typo. Premium cabin trans-Pacific fares are genuinely that expensive, which is precisely why the ChooseFI community treats travel rewards as a core pillar of the FI lifestyle — you're unlocking experiences that would otherwise require years of extra saving. At 90,000 Virgin Atlantic miles for that same seat, your points are delivering **6.7 to 13.3 cents per point (CPP)** in value. To put that in context: most points are considered "good" redemptions at 1.5–2 CPP. This redemption is 4 to 9 times that benchmark. This is what a true sweet spot looks like. ### Why the Gap Exists Virgin Atlantic prices its ANA partner awards using a **fixed award chart** — a relic of the old loyalty program era when airlines published static pricing tables rather than dynamic, revenue-based pricing. ANA's own Mileage Club program charges 75,000–90,000 miles for the same route. Virgin Atlantic's chart prices it at 90,000, but — and here's the critical part — **with zero fuel surcharges on partner-operated flights**. What you see is what you pay. The result is one of the most compelling premium cabin redemptions in all of loyalty programs. The ChooseFI community's founding principle is that every dollar has a job. When 90,000 transferable points can do the job of $12,000 in cash, that's not just travel rewards — that's an asymmetric opportunity you'd be leaving on the table.
